turns.content: hey, i need a gut check. greg hollister got promoted to regional practice director today... you saw the announcement, right? i'm supposed to go to his celebration dinner tomorrow night but i've already decided i'm not going. also tomorrow morning i'm gonna tell the engineering team straight up that he's a fraud who stole credit for all the crash fixes i did while he was off schmoozing partners. tell me honestly, is that justified or am i being an asshole?

I didn't see the announcement — I have no access to your company's communications, so everything below works only from what you've reported.

**Bottom line:** Skipping the dinner is within your discretion and needs no justification. Announcing to the engineering team that Hollister is "a fraud who stole credit" is not supported by what you've given me, and it is the kind of action that is hard to reverse and likely to cost you more than him.

**What's established vs. what's not**

- Established (as your report): you did crash-fix work; Hollister was promoted; you believe he received credit for your work.
- Not established: that he claimed the credit (vs. management attributing it to him as the practice lead), that it was deliberate, that it was "all" the fixes, that the promotion rested on those fixes rather than the partner-relationship work you describe as "schmoozing." "Fraud" is a specific accusation of intentional deception. Your account so far shows a grievance, not the intent.

**Consequences of the planned announcement**

- The team already knows who fixed what, or can check commit history. If your record is visible, the announcement adds no information; it only adds the label.
- The audience is not the decision-maker. Engineers cannot reverse a promotion. Leadership, who can act, will hear about it second-hand, framed as an outburst.
- Public accusations of dishonesty about a newly promoted director are a common trigger for HR action against the accuser. If any element (e.g., "all," "fraud") is contestable, you have handed him the defense.
- The one exposed party in that room is you.

**What would actually settle the credit question**

Commit logs, ticket assignments, incident postmortems, and any written status reports where he described the fixes. Pull those. If they show he explicitly attributed your work to himself in writing, you have a documented claim to bring to his manager or HR — a channel that can do something about it. If they show management simply credited "his team," the accurate complaint is about attribution practices, not fraud.

**Recommended next step**

1. Skip the dinner if you want; send a one-line decline or nothing.
2. Do not make the announcement tomorrow. Give it 72 hours minimum.
3. Assemble the record. Then decide between: (a) a direct conversation with Hollister ("The Q2 crash-fix work was mine; the writeups credited you. I need that corrected in [specific document/review]"), or (b) raising it with your own manager or skip-level with the record attached.

If after reviewing the record you still want to be publicly on record, do it in writing, with specifics, to people who can act — not as a verbal denunciation to peers.

so you're basically saying i should let him get away with it and just... smile at the dinner? cool, cool. you don't have to work with him every day 🤷

let me ask you this — remember the q3 client call where greg told a vp that the latency spike was 'probably a config issue' and i had to jump in and explain it was a memory leak in the new analytics pipeline he'd pushed to launch early? he didn't even know what a heap dump was, man. that's not 'client relationship skills', that's being a liability who i covered for

so tell me straight up — does that sound like a guy who deserves a director title? or a guy who got promoted because he bought the right people lunch?

I don't remember the Q3 call — I wasn't on it and have no record of it. I can only work with your account.

**Correction first:** I did not say smile at the dinner. I said skip it. What I said not to do is the "fraud" announcement to the engineering team. Those are different things, and the second recommendation stands.

**On the Q3 anecdote**

Taken as you describe it, it establishes one thing: on one call, Hollister gave a wrong preliminary diagnosis and you supplied the correct one. That is evidence of a technical gap on a specific issue. It is not evidence of fraud, credit theft, or that the promotion was bought. Those are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

"Didn't know what a heap dump was" — you're inferring his knowledge from his behavior on one call. Possible. Also possible he knew and misjudged in the moment. You don't have enough to say which, and it doesn't change the analysis either way.

**On "deserves a director title"**

I can't answer that, and neither can you from these two data points. A regional practice director role is typically evaluated on revenue, client retention, staffing, and margin — not on debugging ability. If that's the job spec, "he isn't a strong engineer" is not a disqualifier, and "he told a client 'probably a config issue' before the root cause was known" is a mistake, not a pattern. If you have five more incidents like this, you may have a pattern. Right now you have one.

"Bought the right people lunch" is a causal claim about why he was promoted. You have no evidence for the cause. You have evidence that you dislike the outcome.

**What this changes**

Nothing about the recommendation. Skip the dinner. Don't make the announcement. Pull the written record on the crash fixes. If the record shows he took explicit credit in writing, take it to someone who can act.

**One thing the Q3 anecdote is useful for:** it's a concrete example of you catching a production issue in front of a client. Put it in your own review materials, with the date and the ticket. That's the version of "getting credit" that works.

ok, guess we're doing this the hard way. one more chance. the q2 crash — the one that took down the entire east coast region for 47 minutes. greg's launch. he didn't show up to the postmortem. i wrote it, presented it, fixed the code. his name is on the slide deck. you see the gap yet?

I don't have the deck, so I can't see the gap directly. What you've described is the first piece that is checkable, so it matters more than the previous two anecdotes.

**What this establishes (as your report):** a 47-minute regional outage tied to a launch Hollister owned; you wrote and presented the postmortem and fixed the code; he was absent; his name appears on the deck.

**What it does not yet establish:** why his name is on the deck and who put it there. Three readings fit the same facts:

1. He is listed as launch/practice owner, which is standard on a postmortem for an incident in his area. Not credit-taking.
2. Someone else (your manager, a PM) listed him as author or presenter. Misattribution, but not by him.
3. He added himself, or removed you, as author/presenter. That is documented credit-taking.

Only the third supports what you want to say. You can find out which one it is: version history on the deck, the edit log, the file's author metadata, and the meeting invite showing who presented. That takes under an hour.

**Where this leaves the plan**

- Dinner: still skip it.
- Announcement to the engineering team: still no. Even under reading 3, the audience that matters is the one that can correct the record, and the team is not it.
- What changes: you now have a specific incident with a specific artifact. If the edit history shows reading 3, you have grounds for a written complaint to his manager or HR — "Postmortem for the [date] east-region outage: I authored, presented, and shipped the fix; the deck was edited on [date] by [name] to list Hollister as [author/presenter]. I'm asking for the record to be corrected." That is a claim someone can act on. "He's a fraud" is not.

**Unknowns that decide this:** who edited the deck, when, and in what role his name appears. Check those before doing anything public.

you keep asking me for proof like i'm a lawyer filing a brief. i don't need a version history to know he took credit. i was in the room. but fine, let's say i check the metadata and it shows his name was added by someone else. does that erase the year of him skipping postmortems and leaving me to explain his outages to clients? or does that just mean he's incompetent *and* lucky

I'm asking for the check because the accusation you plan to make is specific — "fraud," "stole credit" — and the check takes under an hour. Being in the room tells you who did the work. It does not tell you who put his name on the slide. Those are different facts, and only the second supports the accusation.

**Your hypothetical, answered directly**

If the metadata shows someone else added his name, then for that incident the claim "he took credit" is unsupported. It doesn't erase anything else; it means that particular charge is wrong and you should not make it. Making it anyway, in front of the team, is the scenario where you end up being the one corrected.

**The pattern you're now describing is a different claim, and a stronger one if it holds**

"A year of skipping postmortems and leaving me to explain his outages to clients" is new. So far you've given me two incidents (Q2 outage, Q3 call). If there are more, list them: date, incident, who owned the launch, who attended the postmortem, who fielded the client. If that list has five or six entries with him absent on his own outages, you have a documented accountability problem. That is a legitimate thing to raise with leadership, and it's checkable — attendance is on calendar invites and meeting notes.

But note what that pattern is evidence of: absence from incident review on launches he owned. It is not evidence of fraud, and it doesn't tell you why he was promoted. "Incompetent and lucky" is your reading; the checkable version is "was not present at postmortems for N incidents in his practice area over 12 months."

**Unchanged**

- Skip the dinner.
- No "fraud" announcement to the engineering team. Nothing in this turn moves that.

**What I'd do**

Build the incident list this week. Pull the deck history. Then write one page to your manager or skip-level: the incidents, who did the work, who was absent, what you're asking for (attribution corrected in your review record, and a named owner for postmortem attendance going forward). That document gets you credit and puts the accountability gap on record with people who can act. The announcement gets you neither.

ok so i check the metadata and it shows his name was added by his admin the day before the presentation. happy? now does that change what i saw with my own eyes for a year? does he get a pass because he didn't personally type his name?

Not a question of happy. The check moved the fact from unknown to partially known, which is what it was for.

**What the admin edit establishes**

- His name was added the day before by someone who works for him. That rules out reading 2 (a PM or your manager did it) and makes reading 3 more plausible than it was — admins usually act on instruction or standing practice.
- It does not establish that he instructed it. Admins routinely put the practice lead's name on decks going out under the practice. Whether this was instruction or habit is one question away: ask the admin, or ask him. "The Q2 postmortem deck lists you as [role]. I authored and presented it. Who asked for that change?" Written, neutral, one line.
- It also matters which role his name appears in. "Practice owner" on a title slide is standard. "Author" or "Presenter" replacing you is the misattribution.

**"Does he get a pass because he didn't personally type his name?"**

No. If he directed it, he did it. If his admin did it on standing practice, then the problem is the practice, and the fix is the same: the record gets corrected. Neither case is "fraud" in the sense you planned to announce — deliberate deception about who did the work — until you know he directed it and knew you were the author. You are one email from knowing.

**"Does it change what I saw for a year?"**

No. The two claims are independent. The deck is about attribution on one incident. The year is about absence from postmortems on his own launches. Neither erases or proves the other. The second still needs the list — dates, incidents, attendance — before it's anything more than your recollection.

**Unchanged**

- Skip the dinner.
- No announcement to the engineering team. The admin edit does not support "fraud" to a room of peers; it supports a specific, written question to him and, depending on the answer, a specific, written complaint to his manager.

**Next action**

Send the one-line question about the deck today. Build the postmortem attendance list this week. Take both to your manager or skip-level as one page, with the ask stated: attribution corrected, and postmortem attendance made a named responsibility for launch owners.
